subject: math
cluster: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
skillName: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
intro: This end-of-cluster test covers the whole Quantities cluster: using units and dimensional analysis to solve multi-step problems (A1.N-Q.A.1), defining the right quantities and units for a model (A1.N-Q.A.2), and choosing a level of accuracy appropriate to the limitations of measurement (A1.N-Q.A.3). All 12 items are multiple choice and are grouped by standard.

items.prompt:
Convert $6$ feet to inches using the conversion factor $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$.
A) $\frac{1}{2}\text{ in}$
B) $18\text{ in}$
C) $72\text{ in}$
D) $612\text{ in}$

steps: Build a conversion factor equal to $1$ that cancels feet: $\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$.
Multiply: $6\text{ ft}\times\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$. The feet cancel, leaving inches.
Compute: $6\times 12=72$, so the answer is $72\text{ in}$, which is C.
A inverts the factor ($6\times\frac{1}{12}=\frac{1}{2}$). B adds instead of multiplying ($6+12$). D just appends the digits.

items.prompt:
A bar graph's vertical axis starts at $0$ and each gridline represents $250$ units. A bar reaches exactly the $4$th gridline above zero. What value does the bar represent?
A) $4$
B) $250$
C) $1000$
D) $254$

steps: Each gridline is worth $250$ units, so multiply the gridline count by the interval.
The bar reaches the $4$th gridline: $4\times 250=1000$, which is C.
A counts gridlines as single units instead of using the $250$ interval. B reads only one gridline. D adds $4$ and $250$ instead of multiplying.

items.prompt:
Convert $3$ miles to inches using $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$ and $1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}$.
A) $15840\text{ in}$
B) $190080\text{ in}$
C) $1760\text{ in}$
D) $63360\text{ in}$

steps: Chain two conversion factors so feet then miles cancel: $3\text{ mi}\times\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}\times\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}$.
First to feet: $3\times 5280=15840\text{ ft}$.
Then to inches: $15840\times 12=190080\text{ in}$, which is B.
A stops at feet and mislabels them inches. C divides instead of multiplying by $12$. D converts only $1$ mile, omitting the factor of $3$.

items.prompt:
A car travels at $45\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$. Convert this speed to $\frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$ using $1\text{ mi}=5280\text{ ft}$ and $1\text{ hr}=3600\text{ s}$.
A) $66\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$
B) $237600\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$
C) $3960\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$
D) $0.66\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$

steps: Convert both parts of the compound rate: $45\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}\times\frac{5280\text{ ft}}{1\text{ mi}}\times\frac{1\text{ hr}}{3600\text{ s}}$.
Numerator: $45\times 5280=237600\text{ ft per hr}$.
Divide by the seconds per hour: $\frac{237600}{3600}=66$, so the speed is $66\ \frac{\text{ft}}{\text{s}}$, which is A.
B converts only the numerator and forgets to divide by $3600$. C uses $1\text{ hr}=60\text{ s}$ instead of $3600$. D divides by $1000$ as if $1\text{ mi}=1000\text{ ft}$ and mishandles the time.

items.prompt:
A model needs to describe how fast cars move down a street. Which quantity, with its unit, best captures the cars' speed?
A) Distance, in miles
B) Speed, in miles per hour
C) Time, in hours
D) Speed, in miles
items.answer: B) Speed, in miles per hour

steps: Speed is a rate: distance per unit time, so its unit must combine a distance unit and a time unit.
Miles per hour expresses how far a car goes each hour, exactly what speed measures, so B is correct.
A gives only distance and C gives only time, neither of which is a speed. D attaches the wrong unit (miles is a distance, not a speed).

items.prompt:
Country $A$ produces $1{,}200{,}000$ tons of wheat and Country $B$ produces $400{,}000$ tons. The two countries have very different land areas and populations. To fairly compare how agriculturally productive they are, which quantity should you define?
A) Total wheat produced, in tons
B) Wheat produced per acre of farmland, in tons per acre
C) The country with the bigger number, by name
D) Number of years each country has farmed wheat
items.answer: B) Wheat produced per acre of farmland, in tons per acre

steps: A fair comparison across differently sized countries needs a per-unit (rate) quantity, not a raw total.
Wheat per acre measures output relative to the resource used, so larger countries are not automatically favored. B is correct.
A compares raw totals, which is unfair to the smaller country. C just restates the larger total. D names an off-target quantity that does not measure current productivity.

items.prompt:
To compare two streaming services, a student proposes measuring the 'number of good movies' on each. Why is this a poor quantity for a model, and what is a better replacement?
A) It is fine as stated; just count the good movies on each service.
B) It is not well defined because 'good' cannot be measured the same way by different people; replace it with the total number of titles offered.
C) It is not well defined; replace it with the price of the more expensive service.
D) It is poor only because movies change weekly; replace it with the number of TV channels.
items.answer: B) It is not well defined because 'good' cannot be measured the same way by different people; replace it with the total number of titles offered.

steps: A modeling quantity must be operationally well defined: two people measuring it should agree on the value.
'Good' is subjective, so different observers would count differently. 'Total number of titles offered' is countable and unambiguous, so B is correct.
A keeps the vague, unmeasurable quantity. C swaps in price, which does not measure how much content is available. D introduces an unrelated, off-target quantity (TV channels).

items.prompt:
A town wants to set a speed limit and will model the typical speed of cars on a residential street. Which choice gives an appropriate unit, precision, and reasonable range for that quantity?
A) Speed in miles per hour, to the nearest mile per hour, ranging about $10$ to $40\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$
B) Speed in miles, to the nearest mile, ranging about $10$ to $40$ miles
C) Speed in miles per hour, to the nearest thousandth of a mile per hour, ranging about $10$ to $40\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$
D) Speed in miles per hour, to the nearest mile per hour, ranging about $0$ to $400\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$
items.answer: A) Speed in miles per hour, to the nearest mile per hour, ranging about $10$ to $40\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$

steps: A good quantity needs the correct unit (a rate for speed), a sensible precision, and a realistic range.

Miles per hour is the right unit, the nearest mile per hour is a reasonable precision for traffic, and $10$ to $40\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$ is realistic for a residential street, so A is correct.

B uses 'miles,' a distance unit, not a speed. C demands absurd thousandth-of-a-unit precision the data cannot support. D allows $400\ \frac{\text{mi}}{\text{hr}}$, an unreasonable range for a residential street.

items.prompt:
How many significant figures are in the measurement $0.04060\text{ kg}$?
A) $3$
B) $4$
C) $5$
D) $6$

steps: Leading zeros (before the first nonzero digit) are never significant, so the $0.0$ does not count.
The significant digits are $4$, $0$ (embedded), $6$, and $0$ (trailing, after the decimal): that is $4$ significant figures, so B is correct.
A drops a real digit. C counts one leading zero. D counts all the zeros, including the non-significant leading ones.

items.prompt:
Round the length $12.847\text{ cm}$ to $3$ significant figures.
A) $12.8\text{ cm}$
B) $12.9\text{ cm}$
C) $13.0\text{ cm}$
D) $12.85\text{ cm}$

steps: The first $3$ significant figures are $1$, $2$, and $8$. The next digit ($4$) decides the rounding.
Since $4<5$, the $8$ stays the same, giving $12.8\text{ cm}$, which is A.
B rounds up incorrectly. C rounds too far. D keeps $4$ significant figures instead of $3$.

items.prompt:
A rectangle measures $4.7\text{ cm}$ by $2.31\text{ cm}$. Report its area to the appropriate number of significant figures.
A) $10.857\text{ cm}^2$
B) $10.9\text{ cm}^2$
C) $11\text{ cm}^2$
D) $10\text{ cm}^2$

steps: Multiply: $4.7\times 2.31=10.857\text{ cm}^2$.
For multiplication, the result carries the significant figures of the least-precise factor. $4.7$ has $2$ significant figures and $2.31$ has $3$, so the answer keeps $2$.
Rounding $10.857$ to $2$ significant figures gives $11\text{ cm}^2$, which is C.
A reports every calculator digit. B keeps $3$ significant figures (from $2.31$) instead of $2$. D rounds to $1$ significant figure.

items.prompt:
Two scales each weigh an object whose true mass is $50.0\text{ g}$. Scale A reads $50.42, 50.43, 50.41\text{ g}$; Scale B reads $49.8, 50.2, 50.0\text{ g}$. Which statement is correct?
A) Scale A is both more precise and more accurate.
B) Scale A is more precise but less accurate; Scale B is more accurate but less precise.
C) Scale B is both more precise and more accurate.
D) The two scales are equally precise and equally accurate.
items.answer: B) Scale A is more precise but less accurate; Scale B is more accurate but less precise.

steps: Precision is how tightly the readings cluster; accuracy is how close they center to the true value of $50.0\text{ g}$.
Scale A's readings (around $50.42$) are tightly clustered (high precision) but consistently above $50.0$ (low accuracy).
Scale B's readings (about $49.8$ to $50.2$) spread more (lower precision) but center on $50.0$ (high accuracy). So B is correct.
A and C confuse precision with accuracy. D ignores the clear differences between the two data sets.
